content: In savory bakery products, white-colored starchy roots, tubers, and plantains are typically baked, boiled, and drained. Fruits, including all subgroups, are consumed either raw or cooked as they are sourced. Vegetables are categorized into several groups: medium to dark green leafy vegetables, other brassicas (excluding roots and tubers), vitamin A-rich orange vegetables, peppers, tomatoes, immature peas, beans, and other vegetables. These are generally boiled and drained unless specified otherwise, with exceptions for items like raw lettuces, endives, cucumbers, and iceberg lettuce, which are more likely to be consumed raw. Dairy products include milk (fluid), yogurt or fermented dairy (as is), and cheese (as is). Protein foods encompass boiled eggs, legumes/pulses and their flours, boiled soybeans, raw tofu, peanuts, tree nuts, seeds (dry or paste), and various meats such as beef, lamb, mutton, goat, game, pork, poultry, wild birds, liver, and fish. Fish is further divided into small fish eaten with bones and larger fish not consumed with bones, all of which are cooked. For fruits, raw forms are most commonly listed, but exceptions exist for items more likely to be consumed cooked. Food clustering in data sources involves grouping similar items, which is common in food composition databases. For example, cheese may be described generically or with specific details such as Edam cheese, 30% fat, 60% dry matter. When clustering levels differ between item lists and food composition data, matching requires selecting a generic item, a representative food, or creating an average item by combining data from multiple sources. For instance, in the U.S. Food and Nutrient Database for Dietary Studies (FNDDS), a generic item like Cheese, NFS is used when survey respondents report cheese without further specification. In food pattern modeling, clustering reduces data complexity. For example, refined grain foods in the U.S. were grouped into 20 clusters, such as white bread and white rice. Rich national dietary intake data informs clustering decisions, identifying rarely consumed items and selecting representative foods. For instance, mango varieties consumed by fewer than 5% were clustered to represent mangoes as a whole. Matching food items to composition data involves selecting representative items or creating averages. For example, Rice, white was matched to long-grain white rice. In cases where nutrient values were missing, imputations were made based on similar items. For dairy, all fluid milk was matched to whole milk with 3.5% fat, and yogurt was matched to full-fat, unsweetened varieties to avoid calorie constraints in modeling. Cheese matching was challenging due to global variety and poor descriptions in intake data. Generic items from the German food composition database were used when possible, as German milk is generally unfortified. Fish presented the greatest challenge due to species variety, environmental differences, and ambiguous common names. Many fish were matched to unspecified codes. Cooking oils were often poorly described in dietary data. When no information was available, FAO data was used to identify the most commonly consumed oils in a country, which were then substituted for unspecified oils. Average items were calculated for partially specified foods by averaging nutrient values from multiple database entries. For example, maize and wheat products were averaged across various forms (e.g., whole grain, refined). For meats, wet-cooked items (boiled, stewed, braised) were prioritized, as these are commonly prepared for infants and young children. Lean items were selected based on fat content, and averages were derived across selected items. For fortified items like multiple-micronutrient powders (MNPs), small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS), and fortified infant cereals, nutrient content was determined based on specifications from UN agencies or food aid commodities. Missing values for nutrients like carbohydrate, fiber, and choline were imputed based on ingredient composition. Handling missing nutrient data involved imputing values only when necessary, such as for small subgroups or heavily weighted items. For example, choline was imputed for unfortified items in the German database using USDA data. For small fish, fatty acids and tryptophan were imputed from similar items. In summary, the methodologies described emphasize careful clustering, matching, and imputation to address the heterogeneity and gaps in food composition data, ensuring accurate representation and analysis in dietary studies.
